notes: Replaced r5 interface-extends-incompatible-member and type-alias-reopening-error to avoid repeating the intersection-conflict and interface-merging distinctions. Replaced r6 unconstrained-generic-property-access to avoid mirroring the length-constraint card. Replaced r8 conditional-never-input with a directly documented true-branch indexing fact.

cards.statement: `number[] | string` permits `.slice(0, 3)` before narrowing.
cards.explanation: Both `number[]` and `string` have a compatible `slice` method, so the call is valid on their union.

cards.statement: A value of type `string | number` is directly assignable to `string`.
cards.explanation: A `string | number` value might be a number. TypeScript requires narrowing before assigning that value to `string`.
cards.misconception: A union value is assignable to any one of its member types.

cards.statement: For `{ id: string } | { id: number }`, reading `id` gives `string | number`.
cards.explanation: Both union members expose `id`; a read can produce either member's property type.

cards.statement: `{ id: string } & { active: boolean }` accepts an object with just `id`.
cards.explanation: The intersection combines both object requirements. A value also needs the `active` property.
cards.misconception: An object intersection accepts a value satisfying either side.

cards.statement: In `{ id: string } & { id: number }`, `id` has type `never`.
cards.explanation: The intersected property would need to be both `string` and `number`; its resulting type is `never`.

cards.statement: `string & number` gives a value both string and number methods.
cards.explanation: `string & number` is uninhabitable: no value satisfies both primitive types. TypeScript reduces such an intersection to `never`.
cards.misconception: Intersecting incompatible primitives combines their capabilities into a usable value.

cards.statement: An interface that extends another keeps the inherited properties in its own type.
cards.explanation: An interface's `extends` clause brings in the base type's members. Values of the derived interface still need those members.

cards.statement: An interface can extend one other interface at a time.
cards.explanation: An interface can list multiple types in its `extends` clause and inherit members from each.
cards.misconception: Interface extension is limited to one base interface.

cards.statement: Two declarations of the same interface automatically combine their distinct properties.
cards.explanation: Interface declaration merging joins members from declarations with the same name into one interface.

cards.statement: Ordinary overload groups in merged interfaces place earlier declarations first.
cards.explanation: Merged interfaces place later overload groups before earlier groups. Signatures with a single string literal parameter have a separate ordering rule.
cards.misconception: Merged method overloads retain declaration-group order from earliest to latest.

cards.statement: A type alias can name a union such as `string | number`.
cards.explanation: A type alias can name a union type, making the same union reusable through an identifier.

cards.statement: A type alias for `string` creates a distinct assignability type.
cards.explanation: An alias is another name for its target type. `type UserId = string` remains assignable from an ordinary string.
cards.misconception: A type alias creates a nominally distinct type.

cards.statement: `identity<T>(x: T): T` preserves the argument's type in its return type.
cards.explanation: The same type parameter connects the input and result, preserving the caller's type information.

cards.statement: A call to `identity<T>(x: T): T` requires `T` in angle brackets.
cards.explanation: TypeScript can infer `T` from the value argument. An explicit type argument is optional when inference succeeds.
cards.misconception: Generic function calls require explicit type arguments.

cards.statement: A function instantiates its generic `T` with `new T()` inside the body.
cards.explanation: `T` names a type, not a runtime constructor. A generic factory receives a constructor value, such as a parameter typed `new () => T`.
cards.misconception: A generic type parameter is available as a constructor at runtime.

cards.statement: A `T extends { length: number }` constraint permits reading `.length` from `T`.
cards.explanation: The constraint guarantees a numeric `length` member for values of `T`, so the generic function body may read it.

cards.statement: In `K extends keyof T`, a key must belong to `T`'s properties.
cards.explanation: `keyof T` restricts `K` to keys of `T`; a key absent from that type fails the constraint.

cards.statement: An interface can put `<T>` on a call signature for calls with different argument types.
cards.explanation: A generic call signature declares its own type parameter, allowing the interface to describe a function that is generic at each call.

cards.statement: A static property of `class Box<T>` uses `T` as its declared type.
cards.explanation: A generic class's static members cannot use its type parameter. The class is generic over its instance side.
cards.misconception: A generic class type parameter is available to static members.

cards.statement: An instance property declared as `T` in `class Box<T>` has type `string` in `Box<string>`.
cards.explanation: Substituting `string` for the class type parameter makes an instance property declared as `T` a `string` property.

cards.statement: A defaulted type parameter fills in when inference finds no candidate.
cards.explanation: If inference cannot choose a type argument, TypeScript uses that parameter's declared default.

cards.statement: A `const` type parameter changes inference for a variable passed by name.
cards.explanation: The `const` modifier affects inference for literal expressions written at the call site. A previously declared variable retains its existing inferred type.
cards.misconception: Const type parameters retroactively give named arguments const-like inferred types.

cards.statement: `function first<T extends any[]>(a: T) { return a[0]; }` infers its return type as `T[number]`.
cards.explanation: TypeScript resolves `a[0]` through the `any[]` constraint in this function, so its inferred return type is `any`.
cards.misconception: Indexing a generic array constraint preserves the element type of each call.

cards.statement: For `filter<T, F extends (x: T) => boolean>`, callers can specify just `T` and infer `F`.
cards.explanation: With both parameters required, a caller supplying `T` explicitly also has to supply `F`. The extra parameter prevents partial specification in this signature.
cards.misconception: A call can explicitly provide one required type argument and infer the next one.

cards.statement: `keyof { id: string; active: boolean }` is `"id" | "active"`.
cards.explanation: `keyof` produces a union of the object type's property keys.

cards.statement: `keyof` reduces a string index signature to the `string` type.
cards.explanation: For a string index signature, `keyof` is `string | number`. Numeric property access also reaches string-keyed properties.
cards.misconception: A string index signature gives `keyof` exactly `string`.

cards.statement: For `let item: { id: number }`, `typeof item` in a type is `{ id: number }`.
cards.explanation: In a type position, `typeof item` queries the type of the variable rather than producing JavaScript's runtime type string.

cards.statement: A type-position `typeof` evaluates a function call to determine its type.
cards.explanation: Type-position `typeof` accepts identifiers or their properties, not a call expression. Use `typeof fn` to refer to a function's type.
cards.misconception: A type query can execute or inspect a function call expression.

cards.statement: `{ id: number; name: string }["id"]` is `number`.
cards.explanation: An indexed access type looks up the property's declared type; the `id` property is numeric.

cards.statement: Indexing an object type with a union of keys intersects the property types.
cards.explanation: An indexed access using a union of keys produces a union of the corresponding property types.
cards.misconception: Looking up several keys combines their value types with an intersection.

cards.statement: `string[][number]` produces the array element type `string`.
cards.explanation: Using `number` as the index type of an array retrieves the type of its elements.

cards.statement: Template literal unions pair members positionally.
cards.explanation: Template literal types combine every member of one interpolated union with every member of another. Two two-member unions produce four combinations.
cards.misconception: Template literal types zip union members by their positions.

cards.statement: `Uppercase<"api-key">` is `"API-Key"`.
cards.explanation: `Uppercase<"api-key">` produces `"API-KEY"`; it uppercases characters throughout the string.
cards.misconception: Uppercase changes just the first character of each word segment.

cards.statement: `Lowercase<"HTTP_2">` is `"http_2"`.
cards.explanation: `Lowercase<StringType>` converts uppercase characters throughout a string literal type; the underscore and digit remain unchanged.

cards.statement: `Capitalize<"hello world">` is `"Hello World"`.
cards.explanation: `Capitalize<"hello world">` produces `"Hello world"`; it changes the string's first character, not each word.
cards.misconception: Capitalize performs title casing across words.

cards.statement: `Uncapitalize<"URLPath">` is `"uRLPath"`.
cards.explanation: `Uncapitalize<StringType>` lowercases the first character; the remaining uppercase letters retain their casing.

cards.statement: `number extends string ? "yes" : "no"` is `"no"`.
cards.explanation: A conditional type selects its second branch when the type on the left of `extends` is not assignable to the type on the right.

cards.statement: `T extends Array<infer Item> ? Item : T` extracts `number` from `number[]`.
cards.explanation: `infer Item` captures an array's element type when the array matches `Array<infer Item>`.

cards.statement: `T extends (...args: never[]) => infer R ? R : never` infers the parameters as `R`.
cards.explanation: `infer R` appears in the function's return position, so it captures the return type. For `() => number`, `R` is `number`.
cards.misconception: An inferred type after the function arrow captures its parameters.

cards.statement: `ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never` maps `string | number` to `string[] | number[]`.
cards.explanation: Because the conditional checks a generic type parameter, it distributes over the union and makes a separate array type for each member.

cards.statement: `[T] extends [any] ? T[] : never` maps `string | number` to `string[] | number[]`.
cards.explanation: Wrapping both sides of `extends` in tuples stops distribution. The result for `string | number` is `(string | number)[]`.
cards.misconception: A tuple-wrapped conditional still distributes over a union.

cards.statement: In `T extends { message: unknown } ? T["message"] : never`, the indexed access is valid.
cards.explanation: The true branch knows that `T` has a `message` property, so `T["message"]` is a valid indexed access there.

cards.statement: `{ [K in keyof T]: boolean }` keeps `T`'s original property value types.
cards.explanation: This mapped type keeps the keys while giving the resulting properties the value type `boolean`.
cards.misconception: Mapping over keys preserves each property's original value type regardless of the mapped value expression.

cards.statement: `{ +readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }` makes `T`'s properties readonly.
cards.explanation: The `+readonly` mapping modifier adds the readonly restriction to the generated properties.

cards.statement: `-readonly` in a mapped type leaves readonly properties unchanged.
cards.explanation: The `-readonly` mapping modifier removes readonly from generated properties, making them writable in the resulting type.
cards.misconception: A negative mapping modifier leaves the original modifier in place.

cards.statement: `[K in keyof T]+?` makes existing required properties optional.
cards.explanation: The `+?` mapping modifier adds optionality to generated properties. TypeScript also treats an unprefixed `?` as `+?`.

cards.statement: `[K in keyof T]-?` removes optional properties from the mapped type.
cards.explanation: The `-?` modifier removes the optional flag, not the property. Previously optional properties remain present and become required.
cards.misconception: Removing an optional modifier removes the property itself.

cards.statement: A mapped type's `as` clause changes property values.
cards.explanation: The `as` clause remaps generated property keys. The expression after the colon determines their value types.
cards.misconception: Mapped-type key remapping changes the property value types.
